title: Apocalyptic beasts and the Lamb
summary: Daniel 7 retells the line of empires in the language of beasts, and the "little horn" foretells a religious-political power active through a period of 1260 day-years (Dan 7:25; Rev 12; 13). This is a prophecy about domination and persecution - but its heart is the Lamb, who conquers and takes possession of the eternal kingdom.

sections.heading: Four beasts: the same history, a different language

items.comment: Daniel sees four beasts coming up out of a stormy sea. This is a different picture of the same line of history sketched by the statue of Daniel 2.

questions.text: Why does God tell the same truth about history twice, in different images?

items.comment: The angel gives the key directly: "these great beasts are four kings." The symbol is explained by the text itself - we are not guessing.

questions.text: What gives us certainty that the beasts mean powers, and not whatever happens to come to mind?

items.label: Beasts = empires: the same line as the statue of Dan 2
items.content: Daniel 7 does not introduce a new history, but the same sequence of powers sketched out by Nebuchadnezzar's dream in Daniel 2 (Dan 2:38-40 names the first kingdom explicitly). The historicist reading sees in the four beasts a succession of empires leading all the way to the eternal Kingdom of God. The signal of succession is in the very words of the text: "after you will arise," "another, a second," "then," "a fourth" (Dan 2:39; 7:5-7). This is not speculation, but a reading in keeping with the internal logic of the prophecy.

items.comment: The lion, the bear, and the leopard correspond to the successive kingdoms of Daniel 2 - the pattern repeats and is confirmed. Two prophecies bear witness in agreement.

questions.text: How does the agreement of two independent visions strengthen trust in the prophetic word?

items.comment: Daniel 8 brings two of these powers into closer view with new images: a ram with two horns, and after it a swift goat that defeats it, then itself grows great and breaks into four parts. This is a "close-up" of the middle stretch of the same history.

questions.text: Why does God bring precisely these links of history into closer view in a separate vision?

items.comment: Here too the text explains itself: "the ram... is the kings of Media and Persia," and "the goat is the king of Greece." The prophecy names the empires by name - long before they appeared in that role.

questions.text: What does it mean for trust in the Bible that the prophecy names the powers in advance, by name?

items.label: Daniel 8: the ram and the goat, and a "little horn" toward the sanctuary
items.content: The vision of Daniel 8 overlaps with Daniel 7, but shifts the emphasis: after the ram (Medo-Persia) and the goat (Greece), a "little horn" again grows up, this time turned against "the sanctuary" and its ministry (Dan 8:9-12). The climax is the announcement: "unto two thousand three hundred evenings-mornings, then the sanctuary will be cleansed" (Dan 8:14) - a bridge to the prophetic time calculations (see study 23) and to the theme of the judgment. Three visions (Dan 2, 7, 8) bear witness in agreement: the same history, a rising sharpness, the same God who rules over time.

questions.text: How do three independent visions (the statue, the four beasts, the ram and the goat) together strengthen one message about God's control over history?

items.comment: The fourth beast is "terrifying and powerful," different from the others, with ten horns - a picture of a power that will break apart into many pieces.

questions.text: What does it mean that the fourth power is "different" from all the earlier ones?

items.label: Ten horns: an empire that breaks apart
items.content: Already in the early Church, Christian writers (such as Irenaeus and Hippolytus) linked the fourth kingdom of Daniel 2 and 7 with Rome and expected its division into ten parts - the image of the ten horns (Dan 7:7,24; cf. Rev 17:12). The "difference" of the fourth beast and its fragmentation form the backdrop against which the "little horn" appears (Dan 7:8). The prophecy thus paints not an abstract evil, but a concrete historical arrangement: after the breakup of a mighty empire, a new power of a different character grows up.

sections.heading: The little horn: a religious-political power and the 1260 period

items.comment: From among the horns grows a "little horn" with "eyes like the eyes of a man and a mouth speaking great things." This is not another empire, but a power of a religious-political character, acting through the word.

questions.text: What do "a mouth speaking great things" suggest - where should we look for this power's activity: in an army or in teaching?

items.label: "Little" means a different kind of power, not a different empire
items.content: The horn is "little" not because it is insignificant, but because its strength lies elsewhere than in the armed might of the previous beasts. "Eyes like the eyes of a man" and "a mouth speaking great things" point to intelligence and the authority of the word - a power that acts through teaching and claims, and not by the sword alone. Paul independently describes a similar profile: the "man of lawlessness" seated "in the temple of God" (2 Thess 2:3-4), that is, a usurpation within the spiritual sphere. Together, Daniel and Paul draw one warning.

items.comment: The little horn "speaks against the Most High," "intends to change the times and the Law," and acts through "a time, times, and half a time." This is a critique of a system and of false teaching - not a condemnation of people.

questions.text: What is the difference between an institution's "changing of God's Law" and obedience to God Himself?

items.label: the "little horn": a critique of a system and a teaching, not people
items.content: The traits of the little horn (Dan 7:8,25) are a description of the ROLE and TEACHING of a certain religious-political power: it speaks "against the Most High," claims for itself the right to change God's Law and times, and persecutes the faithful. The historic reading applies this to a system that, after the fall of Rome, joined spiritual power with secular power. The key hermeneutical and ethical principle: prophecy evaluates a SYSTEM and a DOCTRINE, never individual believers, among whom in every age there are sincere followers of Christ. Sola scriptura: the measure is agreement with Scripture, not human tradition or the authority of an institution.

items.comment: "A time, times, and half a time" is expressed by Revelation as a number: 1260 days. By the "day for a year" principle, this is a long period of domination, during which God's people are at times "in the wilderness."

questions.text: What does the picture of the Church protected "in the wilderness" during a time of distress mean?

items.label: "a time, times, and half a time" = 1260 (Dan 7:25; Rev 12:14)
items.content: The Aramaic/Greek expression "a time, times, and half a time" breaks down into 1 + 2 + ½ = 3.5 "times." Revelation explains the same period as 1260 days (Rev 12:6) and 42 months (Rev 13:5) - all three figures are equivalent (42 x 30 = 1260). By the "day for a year" principle (see study 23) this means a long historical period of domination by the "little horn" power. The consistency of three independent figures is an argument for a symbolic, not a literal, reading.

items.comment: The same period is described here as "a time, times, and half a time" - exactly the language of Daniel 7:25. Revelation deliberately alludes to Daniel.

questions.text: What does it give us that Daniel and Revelation describe the same period with the same words?

items.comment: The beast of Revelation 13 "speaks haughty and blasphemous things" and acts for "forty-two months" - again 1260 days. The same profile of power and the same period recur.

questions.text: Why does it matter that the prophecy denounces blasphemous teaching, and not specific people?

items.label: The seal of God and the mark of the beast: two marks of belonging
items.content: Revelation draws a clear contrast: the seal of God on the foreheads of His people (Rev 7:2-3) versus the mark of the beast on the forehead or the hand (Rev 13:16-17). The seal is identified with the name of the Lamb and of His Father (Rev 14:1) - a mark of character and of belonging to the Creator, not a magical stamp. The whole matter is decided in the sphere of worship: to whom we bow down. The number 666 (Rev 13:18) is defined as "the number of a man" - a symbol of human usurpation and imperfection (six, which still falls short of the fullness of seven), and not an invitation to speculate about individuals.

items.comment: Paul independently foretells a "man of lawlessness" who "will take his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God." This is a warning against usurpation in the spiritual sphere - from within, not only from outside.

questions.text: What is more dangerous to faith: persecution from outside, or falsehood that disguises itself as truth?

items.label: "Changing the times and the Law" and worship (Dan 7:25)
items.content: The phrase "he will intend to change the times and the Law" points to interference with God's commandments - including the one that itself appoints "time" (the commandment about the Sabbath, Ex 20:8-11; cf. the study on creation and judgment). The prophecy does not call for indignation against people, but for a return to God's pattern of worship. The theme is developed by the three angels' messages: "worship the Creator" (Rev 14:7) - a positive call, not an attack. The details of identification remain to be confirmed at review.

sections.heading: The Lamb conquers and takes the kingdom

items.comment: The scene changes abruptly: the "Ancient of Days" takes His seat, the books are opened - a judgment is held. Above every usurpation there is a higher Court.

questions.text: What does it mean for the oppressed that above every earthly power sits God's Court?

items.comment: The "Son of Man" comes to the Ancient of Days and receives "dominion, glory, and a kingdom" that "will not pass away." This is Jesus - to Him belongs the final word, not to the little horn.

questions.text: How does our view of the powers of this world change once we know to whom the eternal kingdom belongs?

items.label: "Son of Man": the title by which Jesus named Himself
items.content: The expression "one like a Son of Man" from Daniel 7:13-14 became in the Gospels Jesus' favorite self-designation. By quoting this very scene before the Sanhedrin (cf. Matt 26:64; Mark 14:62), Jesus acknowledged that He is the One who comes with the clouds and receives the eternal kingdom. Revelation repeats this image: "one like a Son of Man" appears at key points (Rev 1:13; 14:14). Thus Daniel 7 becomes a bridge connecting the judgment in heaven with the person of Christ.

items.comment: The kingdom is at last "given to the people of the saints of the Most High." The persecuted do not lose - they inherit. This is the point of the whole chapter.

questions.text: What hope does it give that God's people end not as victims, but as heirs of the kingdom?

items.comment: In heaven the conqueror turns out to be not a predator, but "a Lamb as though it had been slain." God conquers not by the violence of the beast, but by sacrifice - this is the heart of the great controversy.

questions.text: What does it say about God that His symbol of victory is a Lamb, and not a beast?

items.label: "Lamb" (arnion) - victory through sacrifice, not violence
items.content: Revelation consistently calls Christ "the Lamb" - using a Greek diminutive word; it recurs in the book nearly thirty times, becoming its chief title for Christ. This is a deliberate paradox: over against the terrible beasts from the sea and the earth, the central figure of heaven is "a Lamb as though it had been slain" (Rev 5:6). He conquers not by the strength of a predator, but through His sacrifice; His followers conquer "by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony" (Rev 12:11). This overturns the human notion of power.

items.comment: When the powers "make war on the Lamb, the Lamb will conquer them, for He is Lord of lords." The outcome of the great controversy is settled - in the Lamb's favor.

questions.text: Since the end is certain, how do you want to choose your side in this conflict today?

items.label: "the Lamb and those with Him": a shared victory (Rev 17:14)
items.content: Revelation does not end with the Lamb alone - at His side stand the "called, chosen, and faithful" (Rev 17:14). The victory of Christ becomes the portion of His people: those "with His name and His Father's name on their foreheads" on Mount Zion (Rev 14:1). God's response to the work of the beast is not retaliation, but the positive call of the three angels: "fear God... worship the Creator" (Rev 14:6-7). The heart of the prophecy, then, is not fear, but a call to take one's stand on the side of the One who has already conquered.

application.text: Daniel 7 was not given to frighten, but to prepare and to comfort. Yes, the prophecy speaks bluntly of a power that distorts the truth and persecutes the faithful - and this must not be watered down. But the final scene belongs neither to the beast nor to the little horn: it belongs to the Lamb and to the "people of the saints," who inherit the kingdom. The conflict is not won by violence, but by faithfulness to the One who has already conquered. We critique false teaching - but never people; on both sides of the conflict God is seeking hearts.
application.challenge: This week, read Daniel 7 and Revelation 12 side by side and write down the shared motifs (the 1260 period, persecution, victory). Then test one of your "obvious" beliefs of faith with the question "does this follow from Scripture, or only from tradition?" - and ground it on the Word.
